lesson.title: The Cell's Electron Shuttle Buses
lesson.summary: NADH and FADH2 are the reduced, electron-carrying forms of NAD+ and FAD that ferry high-energy electrons collected throughout glycolysis and the Krebs cycle to the electron transport chain.
lesson.body:
NADH and FADH2 are best understood as reusable shuttle vehicles rather than as fuel themselves. Each one is the reduced form of a coenzyme, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide for NAD+ and NADH, flavin adenine dinucleotide for FAD and FADH2, that can pick up a pair of high-energy electrons, along with a proton or two, at one location in the cell and drop them off at another. This is straightforward redox chemistry: NAD+ and FAD are oxidizing agents that become reduced, gaining electrons, whenever they strip electrons away from a substrate being oxidized, exactly the pattern behind every redox reaction covered earlier in this course.

Tracing where each carrier is actually produced makes their bookkeeping much easier to remember. Glycolysis produces 2 NADH per glucose, generated when G3P is oxidized during the payoff phase. Pyruvate oxidation produces another 2 NADH, one for each pyruvate converted to acetyl-CoA. The Krebs cycle is the richest source by far: each single turn produces 3 NADH and 1 FADH2, and because the cycle turns twice per glucose, that comes to 6 NADH and 2 FADH2. Adding everything together, one glucose molecule fully processed through glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, and two turns of the Krebs cycle yields a total of 10 NADH and 2 FADH2, the complete set of electron carriers available to feed the electron transport chain.

NADH and FADH2 are not interchangeable in value, and the difference matters for calculating ATP yield. NADH delivers its electrons to Complex I of the electron transport chain, entering at a relatively high energy level and enabling proton pumping at Complexes I, III, and IV. FADH2 delivers its electrons to Complex II instead, entering the chain at a lower energy level and therefore contributing to proton pumping only at Complexes III and IV. Because FADH2's electrons skip Complex I's proton pumping entirely, each FADH2 ultimately supports the synthesis of less ATP than each NADH does, a consequence purely of where in the chain each carrier hands off its cargo.

There is also a location problem worth understanding. The Krebs cycle and pyruvate oxidation happen inside the mitochondrial matrix, so their NADH and FADH2 are already positioned right next to the electron transport chain. Glycolysis, however, happens in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondria entirely, so its 2 NADH cannot simply diffuse across the mitochondrial membrane to reach Complex I. Cells solve this with shuttle systems that transfer the electrons, though not necessarily the exact same NADH molecule, into the matrix, a detail that turns out to affect the total ATP yield calculation covered next.

Finally, every NAD+ and FAD molecule is reusable; a cell has a limited, finite pool of each, not an unlimited supply. Once NADH and FADH2 deliver their electrons at the electron transport chain, they are oxidized back to NAD+ and FAD and returned to circulation, ready to accept another pair of electrons from the next round of glycolysis or the Krebs cycle. This recycling is precisely why oxygen availability governs so much of metabolism: without a functioning electron transport chain to reoxidize these carriers, the finite pool of NAD+ runs out, glycolysis grinds to a halt, and the cell must fall back on fermentation just to keep regenerating enough NAD+ to survive.
